newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seems unruffled by stocks' rise.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seems unruffled by stocks' rise.

text.p: President Bill Clinton seemed unruffled on Thursday by the stock market's surge past 7,000, saying the economy itself has performed well and enjoys prospects for further growth with low inflation.
The Dow Jones industrial average rose 60.81 points to 7,022.44, the first time it has closed above 7,000.
"The market has produced a remarkable growth, but the economy is growing," Clinton said at a joint news conference with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is visiting the United States.

"Obviously, the concern is whether returns to stocks, returns to investment, are greater than can be justified based on the productivity and profit prospects of the companies that are being traded," he said.

"But if you look at the stability and the growth that we have enjoyed and the prospects we have for stable growth with no inflation, it's hard to say that it's completely out of the question," he added.

Historically, Clinton has been very cautious in commenting on the stock market, and he prefaced his remarks on Thursday by saying, "My own view is that anything we say about this is likely to either have no effect or an adverse one."
Clinton said one reason for the stock markeet rise was that increasing numbers of Americans' own stocks, either directly or through their retirement investments and mutual funds.
While choosing his words carefully, he did not seem unduly concerned about the market's dizzying rise, joking that it stood at 3,200 when he took office.
"Some people say: 'Gosh, we don't want another 1987 here,' but even after 1987 we had a rather rapid rebound," Clinton said, referring to the Oct. 19, 1987, crash.

"So I think what I need to do is try to work on keeping the economy healthy, let's go on and balance the budget, let's invest in our future ... let's follow our strategy and then let the market take care of itself -- as long as there's no destructive element in it. That's what I think we should do," Clinton said.
The tone of his remarks seemd at variance with comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, who suggested in December that there may be some "irrational exuberance" in the financial markets.
Greenspan's statement briefly knocked stock prices down, but they have since resumed their climb.
